title: Activation oscillation & degradation study: INT8 / AWQ / FP8
content:
Purpose:
This note captures an experiment series investigating a recurring failure mode we’ve been seeing in production: transient "activation oscillations" (brief quality drops) and longer-run degradation in token output quality when using aggressive quantization kernels (INT8 / AWQ / FP8) under certain runtime scheduling and kernel fallback scenarios. Goal is to document hypotheses, test matrix, profiling artifacts, preliminary results, and next steps.

Background / motivation:
- Several customers running Dedicated pools at high throughput reported: occasional short bursts of hallucination-like outputs or token-level repetition for a handful of requests per minute. Symptoms align with model outputs produced under quantized kernels (AWQ/GPTQ) and correlated with heavy multiplexing (many concurrent streams) + dynamic kernel switching.
- On the bench, we reproduced lower average log-prob for certain prefixes with AWQ INT8 kernels compared to FP16 baseline. The effect is small but visible on human-eval prompts and amplified on longer context lengths (1k+).

Working hypothesis (multiple, not mutually exclusive):
1) Kernel numerical edge-cases: INT8/AWQ kernels use asymmetric per-channel scales and packed kernel paths that may use different accumulation ordering exposing different rounding behaviors. Small differences can accumulate across many attention steps -> token drift.
2) KV-cache alignment & packing jitter: when requests are sliced for batching or prefetch, the KV alignment (padding bytes) can change kernel execution path or memory layout, causing different rounding order in matmuls.
3) Mixed-precision fallback path: runtime may swap to a different kernel mid-request (e.g., due to transient OOM or scheduler migration). If caching layers assume identical outputs across kernels, drift emerges.
4) Flush / warmup coldness: quantized kernels have slightly different warmup behavior (first few tokens show larger numeric noise); with continuous multi-tenant workloads, we see interleaved cold/hot sequences leading to perceived oscillation.

Experiment matrix (what we ran)
- Models: raven-7b-open (base), raven-13b-compat (decoder-only) patched locally to allow AWQ/GPTQ variants.
- Hardware: H100 PCIe (driver 525), A100-80GB (driver 470) — separate runs to isolate device-specific kernel selection.
- Kernels:
  * baseline: fp16 fused-attn + cublas matmul (reference)
  * int8-awq-packed: AWQ per-channel packing (fused attention when available)
  * gptq-int8-tensor: GPTQ per-tensor quant + row-wise scales
  * fp8-e4m3: experimental FP8 path (NVIDIA kernel)
  * fallback: hybrid path where runtime explicitly swaps to fp16 matmul on OOM detection
- Batch sizes and concurrency: [1, 4, 8, 32] concurrency across 4 request streams, seq-len: [128, 512, 1024, 2048]
- Prompt types: code-completion (structured), summarization (long context), chit-chat (low perplexity), adversarial prefix (high perplexity)
- Metrics collected: token-latency (p95/p99), tokens/sec, per-token logprob delta vs fp16 reference, perplexity on held-out validation set, embedding similarity (cosine) of outputs vs baseline, BLEU/ROUGE for targeted evals, hallucination indicator (manual mark), numeric stability flags from kernels, kernel-switch events and timestamps.

Profiling approach:
- Instrumented runtime to emit kernel selection events (kernel_name, offset, seq_pos, kv_alignment_bytes) to trace logs (lightweight sampling at 1/10 requests).
- Attached nvprof-equivalent counters: L2 hit rate, SM utilization, register spills, shared-memory stalls for kernels.
- Collected CPU-side flamegraphs around scheduler decision times (kernel eviction, OOM fallback), and runtime trace of batching windows.

Key observations (preliminary)
- Activation oscillation is most pronounced when: concurrency >= 8 and seq-len >= 1024 with AWQ-int8-packed kernels.
- Oscillation shows up as short bursts (3-7 tokens) of low-logprob words, often followed by recovery to baseline behavior — suggests non-catastrophic numeric drift not permanent model collapse.
- Kernel switch traces: in many failing requests we see an interleaved pattern: fused-attn-int8 -> fallback-matmul-fp16 -> fused-attn-int8 across the same request (kernel chosen per-layer based on dynamic memory pressure). This correlates strongly with the bursts.
- KV alignment differences: when requests are padded to different batch shapes, the quantized-packed kernels take a distinct code path (packed vs non-packed). The packed path has slightly different accumulation ordering (observed from kernel assembly), consistent with hypothesis #1.
- FP8 path on H100 had lower p99 latency but slightly higher variance and fewer oscillation instances than AWQ int8, but absolute quality vs FP16 was still slightly worse (embedding cosine ~0.986 vs fp16 baseline 1.0).

Representative numeric results (high level):
- On raven-7b-open, seq=1024, concurrency=8, AWQ-int8-packed: avg token-logprob drop = -0.08 nats/token vs fp16 baseline (SD 0.04); FP8-e4m3: drop = -0.05 nats/token (SD 0.03).
- Hallucination bursts: observed in 0.9% of requests with AWQ-int8-packed vs 0.2% fp16 baseline under same load.
- Latency hit: AWQ-int8-packed p95 = 18ms (vs fp16 21ms) — so AWQ is faster and still slightly worse quality. Some customers may accept tradeoff but bursts are concerning.

Deep dive: kernel swap timeline example
- Request start (t0) selected int8-packed kernels for layers 0..10.
- At t1 scheduler preempts some blocks to service a large batch -> temporary memory pressure, runtime triggers fallback for matmuls in layers 11..14 to fp16 to avoid OOM.
- At t2 fallback finishes, runtime re-selects int8-packed for layer 15..end.
- Output shows token-level divergence starting around layer 12 and manifesting in 3 tokens, then correction after layer 17 when all subsequent matmuls used same kernel type.
- Interpretation: partial-layer kernel heterogeneity introduces small per-layer rounding differences that combine non-linearly in the softmax/attention path, creating transient token drift.

Open questions / things to test next
- Can we make the runtime prefer kernel-stickiness per-request (force single kernel family end-to-end) when latency headroom is sufficient? Measure cost of forcing fp16 vs risk of oscillation.
- Quantize-aware KV alignment: can we ensure padding alignment invariants so kernel packing choice is deterministic across batch shapes?
- Fine-grained numeric mitigation: introduce per-layer stochastic rounding or small additive bias correction to packed kernel accumulators to cancel systematic drift.
- Is there a model-architecture dependency (rwkv vs decoder-only transformers vs llama-family)? Run on a small set of structural variants.

Immediate mitigations suggested for staging/production
- Add runtime flag: request-level kernel-consistency: mode=[best-effort | strict-stickiness | force-fp16-on-fallback]. Default best-effort. Push strict-stickiness to Dedicated customers as opt-in.
- Detect kernel-switch events mid-request and raise a quality-regression alert (counter + sample capture) for immediate forensics.
- Expand flamegraph sampling for high-risk pools (concurrency>8 & seq>512) and keep 1% request traces for 24h for debugging.

Notes to self / TODOs
- Replicate with GPTQ-int8-tensor variant (per-tensor) to see if row-wise vs channel-wise quantization matters.
- Add embedding-similarity thresholds into production anomaly detector.
- Run long-run soak test (24h) with forced kernel-switching to measure frequency of permanent degradation (none seen so far).
- Share a short ticket/one-pager with Solutions Eng + CS for customers observed to have issues.

Appendix: quick commands used
- perf harness: ./tools/perf_runner --model raven-7b --kernel awq-int8 --batch 8 --seq 1024 --concurrency 8 --prompts ./test_prompts/long-context.json --trace kernels,kv_align --out /tmp/awq-run-20260218
- nvprof collect: nsys profile --stats true --output /tmp/nsys-awq-report -- ./runtime/bench 

Bottom line:
- AWQ/INT8 offers attractive latency gains but exposes a mode where mixed-kernel execution within a request can produce short-lived but meaningful quality oscillations. The most straight-forward mitigation is to prefer kernel-consistency per-request and to make packing decision deterministic with respect to KV alignment. We should prioritize a minimal runtime change (stickiness flag + alerting) while exploring numeric mitigation in kernels.
